President’s Column
November! Where has the time
gone. It seems like summer just
ended, but the Christmas season is
just around the corner. Of course,
that means this is the height of craft
show season. Circle Craft Christ
mas Show is coming up soon, and
with it our Guild demonstration.
As a five day show, there are a lot
of spaces to fill, so please contact
Merv Graham and volunteer a little
of your time. As a bonus, you will
get free entry into the best show in
town. This will give you the oppor
tunity to complete your Christmas
shopping early, avoid crowded
malls and get unique gifts for those
on your list. While you are at the
show, stop by our booth and Clau
dia Hayward’s and say hello. Of
course, that visit might show you
the perfect gift for somebody on
your list! Dale Rouleau and Jason
Marlow also have booths at the
show that are well worth a visit.
This year the Circle Craft show also
has glass blowing, blacksmithing,
pottery and, of course, woodturning
demonstrations. In addition to the
guild booth, Dale Rouleau, Jason
Marlow and Dennis will be demon
strating on the main stage.
By the time you read this, the Doug
Fisher demonstration and class will
be over. I hope that you attended
and learned some neat things about
eccentric turning, carving and co
louring. Don’t forget, this month’s
president’s challenge is “decorated”.
Another upcoming guest demon
strator is Anthony Harris in January.
Check our Steve Hanson’s article
on this below, and visit Anthony’s
website at http://acmepipes.com/
index.php. It has the appearance
of a website in the early stages of
creation, but a read over his website
will definitely give you the urge to
meet they guy who came up with
the off-beat content of that site!
Don’t forget to come out to the
November meeting. The demon
stration will be fascinating, educa
tional, and entertaining (in case you
have not realized it, I will be the
demonstrator).

Guitar Hollow Forms by David Wagner
Dennis Cloutier
David’s demonstration was on how
to turn a guitar shaped hollow
form, but his real message was
to let your other passions inspire
your woodturning. David is the
first one to admit that he is not a
musician. In fact, I think he told
me that he couldn’t carry a tune in
a bag. But just the same, music is
important to him, and it has served
as the inspiration for this series of
work.
David starts by cutting out the
guitar shape on the band saw. He
chucks it on the lathe, flattens the
front and hollows out the inside.
He frequently uses inlay or color
ation to decorate the band around
the opening. When he uses dyes
he burns the boundaries of the
coloured area to prevent the dye
from wicking along the wood
fibres. He does this by holding a
burning pen steady, while turning
the workpiece by hand when it is
mounted on the lathe.
Once the top surface is finished,
David uses double sided tape
to mount the piece onto a scrap
block on the lathe. He cautions
against using too much tape as
it can be very difficult to get the
piece off afterwards. Once the
piece is mounted on the lathe he
cuts off the foot and turns a gently
curved profile on the back. He
then sands and finishes the piece.
David’s guitar pieces don’t have
necks, strings or frets. They aren’t
meant to look exactly like guitars,
but instead to suggest them, and
they do that beautifully.
Thanks for a great demo David.

Upcoming Events
Steve Hansen
Anthony Harris Demo and Class
Please mark your calendar for January 22 & 23, 2011.
Anthony Harris, of Kansas, will be visiting the Guild
for a Saturday demonstration and a Sunday class.
Anthony specializes in box making, employing handchased threads in wood and other materials such as
brass, stone, ivory, horn, bone, seeds, sweet potatoes,
banksia pods, plastics, etc. Anthony figures that if you
can thread two materials together, it ought to be more
fun to join three! He also turns architectural repro
ductions, and a lot of natural edge and utility greenwood bowls.
Anthony started turning in 1969 and he has been
teaching and demonstrating since the late ‘70s. His
work is found in many galleries throughout the midwest United States. Anthony has demonstrated twice
at AAW Symposium, thrice at the Southwest Associa
tion of Turners, and at the Utah Woodturning Sympo
sium. From what I’ve learned about Anthony, he is an
entertaining and thought-provoking turner. Anthony’s
motto is: “Keep trying. Never give up. You will al
most always succeed before you run out of wood.”
For the Saturday demonstration, Anthony will make
2 bowls from one log – that sounds like good use of
material! He’ll hand-chase some threads on a box,
perhaps in some unusual materials (hairy acorn?)
and make a pipe. The pipe (Meershaum Calabash) is
complex, requires precision and planning, multi axial,
unusual hardware, and shows techniques that you’ve
likely not seen before – I can hardly wait.
For Classes, please contact Fred Baldwin (fwbaldwin@
hotmail.com) for signup. (Remember, your payment
secures your place. It is first come, first served. Den
nis) The classes can be negotiated through Steve Han
sen (urquell@shaw.ca) as to what your preference is.
Perhaps you want to hand-chase threads, maybe work
with some new material, perfect your green-wood
bowls/spindles – Anthony can split the class into a
couple of groups to accommodate students.
Give yourself an early Christmas gift and sign-up now

Notes from FOF
1. Material : use straight and close grained wood for delicate spindles to avoid
snaps
2. Design : should follow the shape of the receiving object in an harmonious
flow (see www.cindydrozda.com and youtube uploads)
3. Mounting : secure (square) turning blank in a 4 jaw chuck, supporting the
slim end with the tailstock for roughing
4. Speed rule is : 6,000 < diameter(inches)*speed(rpm) < 9,000; so top speed
generally for diameters less than one inch
5. Key concept : proceed from the slim end to the stopper /top base end (i.e.
towards the headstock) in stages, roughing, detailing and finishing at each
stage, so that there is no need to touch up delicate sections which afterwards
have no support. So for a top, the stem is turned first at the tailstock end and then work proceeds on shaping
down the base of the top; similarly with the finial which may end in a stopper for a bottle.
6. Turning tools : 3/8” spindle gouge (or ¼” and ½”) plus a skew and parting tool. Spindle gouge can be the
primary tool, with a skew used to finish the bottom of a bead or a tight corner
7. Toolrest : 1” round bar is useful as can wrap fingers around it, giving support to a delicate stem
8. Turning : basic beads and coves
9. Replication : to make multiple copies, use a story stick, or mark key positions on a tape secured to the
toolrest.
Woodturners’ Liability Insurance
Allan Cusworth
As most of you already know, our Guild’s BC Crafter’s
Association liability insurance covers paid up mem
bers of the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild
only when demonstrating the art of woodturning, or
doing any other woodturning activity, in public at
an event sanctioned by the Guild. Members are only
insured for Liability action arising from this activity
provided the following rules set forth by the insur
ance carrier, have been followed. This information is
provided to the guild by the BC Crafters president, Bill
Olsen.
1. The date, time and location of the demonstration,
or other woodturning activity, has been given to the
Guild Executive; has been approved and placed in
the minutes of a Guild Executive meeting; and has
been provided to the newsletter editor as a events
item. The Executive has the right to refuse the request,
but by accepting and printing the information about
the demonstration has proclaimed this to be a Guild
sanctioned activity and as such the Liability insurance
of the Guild will cover the Guild members involved.
2. This notice of an activity must be provided to the
Executive, or Guild member authorized by the Guild
Executive, before the date of the activity, and the date
provided must be recorded as proof for any insurance
claims that may arise from the demonstration or other
woodturning activity. This is a requirement of the in
surance Carrier to guard against unauthorized claims
being filed from an event.

Tech Talk
Bruce Campbell
We had a good session this month at the Tech Talk
table. Tom started by reporting that he usually cleans
the front filter on his ceiling-mounted dust filter
but took a look inside this time to discover a huge
buildup of dust on the filter bags as well. While some
amount of build-up can actually help in the filtration
process there does come a point where you need to
clean out the bags too.
This led to some discussion about dust filtering:
- Your ceiling mounted dust filter should be located
on one side of the shop to help induce a circular air
flow pattern
- Ceiling filters should be considered your third
line of defense against dust. Remember, the air it is
filtering is the same air you are breathing. The first
line of defense is a good dust collecting system that
picks up dust as it is created and the second defense
is a good personal air filtration system. If you blow
your nose in the shower after a day in the shop you
should not have dust coloured mucus. If you do then
you should revisit your dust collection systems.
Mike wanted to know why there were little holes in
the chin apron of his new AirTrend respirator. Sev
eral people explained that the whole point of per
sonal respirators is that they blow filtered air into the
helmet, which gives you the air to breathe but also
creates a positive pressure inside the mask. The holes
are to allow air to escape so that a constant air flow is
created.
Someone purchased a gouge from Michael Hosaluk
at the symposium but cannot seem to re-create the
grind using a fingernail jig - particularly the flared
wings. We all discussed the various virtues of finger
nail grinds, recommended some adjustments to the
fingernail jig and concluded that perhaps it was no
so important to worry about the wings given that they
are rarely engaged in the average cut.
The next point was a discussion of the grind used to
go across the bottom of a bowl. Everyone agreed
that a steeper grind on the bevel was needed but
there was debate over what profile the grind should
have. I recalled a statement that Stuart Batty made
when he was last here that a “professional” grind was
best. A professional grind is achieved by setting the
bevel angle on a platform and then simply rolling the
gouge while it is held perpendicular to the face of the
wheel. The results in a grind that looks a lot like a
bluntly sharpened pencil. Try it and see.
One person reported that they had a failure with the
Wolverine jig because the gouge wiggled loose while
grinding. Inspection showed that both sides of the
flute were not being held and as the gouge started
to vibrate it slipped loose. In most cases this is just
annoying but sometimes it results in a ruined edge
that needs to be fully re-ground. There is a rare but
very serious risk that this could result in a nasty catch
against the stone causing the stone to chip or even
shatter. There have been serious injuries and even
deaths attributed to injuries from flying pieces of
grinding wheel. Please follow some simple grinder
safety tips:
- Take the time to balance you grinding wheels so
they run smoothly.
- Stand to the side of the grinder as it is spinning up
and while you are grinding.
- Avoid slipping off the sides of the grinding wheel.
- Do not grind on the side of the wheel unless it is
specifically designed for side loading.
We discussed a simple process for reducing side
wobble on a grinder wheel. Loosen the nut and turn
the wheel 1/8 of a turn; tighten the nut and check the
wobble by giving the wheel a small spin by hand (not
under power); if the wobble has not improved then
repeat until you find the “sweet” spot. Then, tighten
the nut without moving the stone. Remember not to
over-tighten the nut as you can crush the stone if you
go too tight.
Another way to stabilize a stone is to buy a pair of
table saw blade stiffeners from Busy Bee Tools. Place

one on either side of the stone and tighten the nut -
you should notice a marked improvement.
We talked about the suggestion that one Symposium
presenter made to reshape the grinding wheels so
they are rounded rather then flat. This should be done
with great care and the stones will need to be rebal
anced afterwards. Then, grind lightly (good advice at
all times) especially on the sides of the stone.
Finally, I reported on the new 8”, 120 grit diamond
wheel that I bought at the symposium. It runs very
smoothly and gives a very smooth finish on the bevel.
But, I would not recommend replacing both wheels
with diamond ones. I suggest keeping a rougher (say
80 grit) stone wheel on the other side for those heavy
grinding jobs.
Happy turning. Be safe and bring you technical ques
tions and insights to the Tech Talk table next month.
